title: The cost of classroom interruptions
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that classroom interruptions cost far more learning than the seconds they occupy, because they leave a 'wake' of lost focus for both students and teacher. He opens with an observed Year 9 lesson in which a 20-second knock at the door derailed an excellent explanation and dissolved the class's concentration. Borrowing the wake metaphor from Peps McCrea, he marshals Kraft and Monti-Nussbaum's 2020 study showing classrooms are interrupted more than 2,000 times a year, costing 10 to 20 instructional days per student. A juggling analogy explains the mechanism: students and teachers hold many ideas in limited attention, and an interruption drops them all. Barton then catalogues twelve interruption types he has seen, many of them teacher-generated, and closes with a call for teachers and leaders to reduce what is within their control. Classified Practice & Culture because the piece's operational target is classroom routines, behaviour and school-level protocols rather than a pedagogy or curriculum question.
points: The 'wake' idea reframes an interruption's cost as the time needed to rebuild the prior state of thinking, not the duration of the interruption itself.

Kraft and Monti-Nussbaum's Providence data are cited: over 2,000 interruptions per classroom per year, over half extending lost time beyond the interruption, and 10 to 20 lost instructional days per student.
Barton stresses that interruptions degrade the teacher's performance too, as seen in the observed teacher's rushed, redundant explanation after resuming.
Many of the twelve catalogued interruptions are self-inflicted, including tangents, praise that breaks silence, and repeated instructions, so they are within the teacher's control.
School leaders are given a specific role: rethinking drop-ins, behaviour policies and equipment-borrowing protocols to protect lesson time.
quotes: First, the teacher had forgotten where she was up to. She looked at the board to remind herself, and made the sensible decision to backtrack a few steps. But as she resumed her explanation, something was different.
Then there were the students. Previously, they were quiet and focussed. Most had, understandably, used the handing over of the books as an opportunity to take a cognitive break.

You see, the thing about interruptions is that they leave a wake. In other words, the learning time lost to an interruption is not just the amount of time the interruption itself takes up, but the time it takes both the student and the teacher to get back to that state of thinking that they were prior to the interruption.

Students can only think about so much at any one time, so as soon as the interruption happens, the balls start to fall to the floor as their limited attention goes elsewhere. Once the interruption is dealt with, it takes time to pick each of those balls back up and get them to the point they were before.

And this doesn't just happen to students. Teaching is an incredibly complex art form. The teacher in the lesson needs all her attention to deliver a high-quality explanation, think hard about her words and her gestures, and adjust things such as pace and the tone of her voice based on the verbal signals she picks up from her students.

Teachers can plan their explanations in advance, have clear rules and routines in place around behaviour and equipment, and try hard to keep quiet once students are focussed. Leaders can think carefully about classroom drop-ins, behaviour policies and the protocols in place for getting equipment from another teacher mid-lesson.

We will never eliminate interruptions entirely. But by being aware of their impact - making students aware too - and making carefully considered adjustments, we might be able to reduce the damage they cause.
